持琴時以手穩握管身，使吹口對準嘴部；若為彎管型，可將管身置於身側，較便於攜帶，也: Hold the instrument firmly by the body with the mouthpiece lined up with your mouth; if it is the curved type, the body can rest at your side, which is easier to carry and keeps the bell from pointing straight at other people. It sounds with a brass-style embouchure: set your lips against the mouthpiece and blow a steady stream of air. For a beginner the first task is a steady hold and embouchure, and practice short, clean attacks; since there are no fingerholes, do not aim at complex melodies at first — the point is to control the airflow and the volume.
盧爾號一詞涵蓋兩類古代氣鳴樂器。青銅製者屬青銅時代，常見成對埋於泥炭沼，出土於丹: The word lur covers two kinds of ancient aerophone. The bronze ones belong to the Bronze Age and are often found buried in pairs in peat bogs, in Denmark and northern Germany, and also in Norway and southern Sweden; Scandinavian rock carvings show them. The wooden ones are later, used in medieval Scandinavia and first recorded in Icelandic sagas, as war horns to gather troops and frighten the enemy; there were also birch-bark horns, used by farmers and dairymaids to call the cattle and to signal. The bronze lur also appears in ancient Greek music. The word survives in modern Swedish, and the Icelandic composer Jón Leifs wrote for the lur in orchestral works.

The lur is an aerophone from Scandinavia, Hornbostel-Sachs number 423.121.22. It is a long natural horn without fingerholes, blown with a brass-style embouchure, and it comes straight or curved; the curve makes it easier to carry and keeps the noise from pointing at bystanders. In ancient times there were two kinds, bronze and wooden: the bronze lur is found in Nordic and ancient Greek use, while the wooden lur serves as a war horn in Icelandic sagas and later as a horn for farmers and dairymaids calling the cattle and passing on signals.
